videos.description:

In the conversation, Bankulli shares his thoughts on why “Grammy is an American award, not a Nigerian award” and why he believes Nigerians should pay more attention to The Headies and what the award represents for the Nigerian music industry.

He also speaks on the importance of respect within the music industry, emphasizing that respect is reciprocal, while reflecting on the recognition artists receive from major award platforms.

Bankulli also discusses Chronicles of Afrobeats and the importance of documenting and preserving the story of Afrobeats.

From Ayra Starr and Wizkid to the evolution of Afrobeats and the future of Nigerian music, Bankulli gives his perspective on the industry and the people shaping it.

videos.description:
In this exclusive exit interview, the BBNaija Season 11 finalists and evictees sit down to share their unfiltered truths about life inside the house and what happened after. Temi Nkem, the winner, opens up about being a gambit, feeling like the luckiest man, and why being emotional was never a weakness but a strength. She also addresses the disconnect between her UK accent and the core fan base, explaining that being Nigerian enough has nothing to do with how she speaks. The conversation then shifts to Sheba, who reflects on being the first female Head of House, dealing with age stereotypes, and the real root of her clashes with Tram: ideologies and the way we perceive things.

The housemates take turns revealing their next moves. Aikou talks about turning his imagination into books and music, while Barry shares his plans in fashion, punditry, and acting. Bluethopia gets candid about being misunderstood, her emotional strength, and her upcoming fashion brand. Ricky explains why he deliberately stirred chaos in the house and addresses the flirting with Sheba. Flora speaks on the difficulty of being a gambit and her beauty business goals. Oyin clears up misconceptions about performing for the cameras and reveals her jewelry and modeling plans. Tram discusses coming fifth, feeling appreciated, and his ambition to take over streaming globally. Temi Nkem also talks about driving in Nigeria, going back to school, and becoming a vlogger.

The interview wraps with Sheba explaining that her arguments with Tram were never about the surface issues but about deeper principles. Aikou shares his Abuja roots, Kogi heritage, and his vision for nationalism and Pan-African unity. This is a must-watch for every BBNaija fan who wants to know what really happened inside the Season 11 house and what these stars are planning next.

videos.title: EXCLUSIVE: Abi and Araga Spill On Nomy's Disqualification, HOH Pressure and Life After BBNaija

videos.description:
Abi and Araga are out of the Big Brother Nigeria house and they are holding nothing back. In this exclusive interview, they open up about their journey from the first night to the final weeks. Abi, the first female Head of House twice, talks about the weight of the crown and how she had to switch her leadership style to keep the house together. Araga opens up about finding his circle, the friendships that mattered, and the moments that tested him.

Then the conversation turns to Nomy. Her disqualification. Did she deserve it? Did they see it coming? Abi says she figured it was going to happen. Araga says her attitude made it obvious. But the real bombshell comes when they are asked about their relationship with Nomy outside the house. Abi says she cannot be friends with someone who ignored her during a task and disrespected the team. Araga says he was never friends with her and does not see that changing. The friendship question gets a hard no from both.

They also talk about who they want to keep in their lives. Gerard and Yusuf are definite for Araga. Cassie gets a mention from Abi but she thought it was fake. Chimsom chuka never aligned. The house was a confined space and most relationships were just for show. Real life is different.

And they reveal their plans after the house. Abi wants to go to pilot school and make enough money to sponsor herself. Araga is a fashion model, actor, entrepreneur and athlete. He runs 100 and 200 meters and dreams of representing Nigeria. He also has an eyewear line called Araga that he has been building for four years.

videos.title: Joshua Baraka: Lagos Feels Like Mini Hollywood & Nana Changed Everything | Midday Show
videos.headline: Joshua Baraka: Lagos Feels Like Mini Hollywood & Nana Changed Everything | Midday Show
videos.description:
Joshua Baraka (the “Nana guy” from 256/Uganda) sits down on The Midday Show at Cool FM 96.9 Lagos for a full, unfiltered conversation about his breakthrough, career growth, and what’s next.
He opens up about the first time he felt “Nana” was real — the song getting played five times in a row in a club/bar while people sang along, kids in the neighborhood singing it, and random people in shops calling him “the Nana guy.” He also talks about Lagos feeling like a mini Hollywood (if Hollywood is iPhone Pro Max, Lagos is iPhone Pro), the high standards on video shoots, and how it inspires him as an East African artist.
Other highlights include:
•  Pressure (or lack of it) after a massive breakout hit and not wanting to be boxed into one sound
•  “Wrong Places” becoming Uganda’s most streamed song in 2025
•  Representing East Africa when he’s often the only one in the room
•  The Recess series (inspired by Kendrick’s The Heart) as a sonic break before albums, the life-cycle concept behind Baby Steps → Growing Pains → Juvie, and what’s coming with Recess Part 2
•  Working with Tiwa Savage on “Commando” (from Recess Part 2, expected around late October), her humility, and the collab process
•  Producing most of his own music, multi-instrumentalist skills (piano, guitar, drums, saxophone), abstract/distorted cover art, Easter eggs for fans, and staying grounded with family, friends, and the Natives of B’rakaland

videos.title: How Salem King Became Nigeria's Ultimate Creator
videos.headline: How Salem King Became Nigeria's Ultimate Creator
videos.description:
​@salemkinging didn’t set out to become a full-time creator.

The son of ministers, Salem grew up in a home that encouraged curiosity, reading and asking questions. He went on to study Economics at university before entering the world of real estate, where he sold some of the most expensive properties in Nigeria’s most exclusive neighbourhoods.

Then, on the side, he started making content.

What began as a creative experiment quickly turned into something much bigger. His content found an audience, went viral and opened up opportunities he hadn't expected. As his platform grew, Salem began teaching others what he had learnt, sharing his knowledge through a series of classes designed to help aspiring creators build their confidence and find their voice.

Eventually, he made the decision to leave his job and pursue content creation full-time.

Today, Salem King is building the Creatorium franchise and positioning himself at the centre of Nigeria's rapidly evolving creator economy.

In this episode, we talk about his childhood, his journey from Economics to real estate, the moment he discovered the power of content, what going viral really changed, leaving a conventional career behind and what it takes to build a sustainable life as a creator.

Before independent rap became a business model, Too $hort was already selling tapes hand-to-hand in Oakland. More than four decades later, Short Dog sits down with Donwill to trace the improbable longevity of a career that helped establish the Bay Area as its own hip-hop universe. He revisits hiding his earliest rhymes from his mother, producing his own records, documenting Oakland when New York and Los Angeles dominated rap's geography, and the run of albums that culminated in Gettin’ It (the record he considers the peak of his original sound) and the moment he got to work with his childhood hero, George Clinton. 

Too $hort explains how relationships with The Notorious B.I.G., Jay-Z, UGK, Eric Sermon and Lil Jon expanded his reach without disconnecting him from the Bay and how “Blow the Whistle,” released deep into an already historic career, effectively bought him another 20 years. Along the way, he talks “raunchy rap”, censorship, protecting young artists from the streets and what it means to be 60 in a genre that once wasn't expected to survive long enough to have senior citizens. For Too $hort, the answer has been sitting in the title of his earliest project all along: don't stop rapping.  Too $hort breaks down:

How selling tapes independently in Oakland became the foundation for a 40-plus-year career
Why Gettin’ It represents the peak of his original Bay Area sound and what working with George Clinton meant to him
How Biggie, Jay-Z, UGK, Eric Sermon and Lil Jon helped open new chapters without changing who he was
Why “Blow the Whistle” became the late-career anthem that gave him another 20 years
What hip-hop can learn about longevity, protecting the bag and growing old without leaving the culture behind

videos.title: Fola Interview: Football Dreams, Davido/ Drake Dream Collab & Why He Believes Anything Is Possible
videos.headline: Fola Interview: Football Dreams, Davido/ Drake Dream Collab & Why He Believes Anything Is Possible
videos.description:
Fola is not your typical lover boy and he is setting the record straight. In this exclusive interview on the Midday show with Abi, he opens up about his new album, his approach to love songs and why he does not rush things anymore. "I know how to narrate love stories very well," he says. "I'm not much that deep of a lover boy like that."

He talks about his song My Type and how it is really a body positivity anthem. "Whatever sort of body type you have, you're beautiful just the way you are." He also speaks on his brotherhood with BNXN and whether an EP together is possible. "BNXN is my brother. Shout out to BNXN." He even reveals that he used to play football actively until he broke his arm. Would he have been a richer footballer than an artist? "I know how to sing more than I know how to play football."

The conversation gets deep when he talks about success and faith. "You can't tell me that nothing is impossible. That's just what I know." He believes Nigerians limit themselves and it is his responsibility to show people that anything can happen. He also reveals he would love a Fola and Drake song and has even written something for it. "When your dreams are too big, they laugh at you."

He also breaks down how 2am in Toronto came together. He recorded it a while ago, stumbled upon it in his archives while on tour in Canada, and reached out to OBO Baddest who picked it and sent it back the same night. The rest is history.
